title: Real and fictitious threats
origin: map-v1.1 (idea named in MAP11 §3 without an id; the id SAF.FICTITIOUS is ours)

D0.outcome: Explains the difference between a capture that gains something after best play and one that only looks possible, and gives one reason a capture can be fictitious (pin, discovered line, recapture).

D1.outcome: In positions where a piece is attacked, says whether the attack is real and states the reason when it is not.

D2.outcome: In a mixed set that includes harmless moves, says for each of the opponent's last moves whether it threatens anything, without being told to look for a bluff.

D3.outcome: Finds the quiet move that makes the opponent's real threat fictitious (removing the checking line or the pinned target) and says what it costs in tempo; rejects it when the threat could not be carried out anyway.

misconceptions: A threat that cannot be executed now can be ignored for good (the position changes and the same capture may work three moves later).
A preparatory move to disarm a threat is always a wasted tempo.
conditions: A threat is real if carrying it out gains something against best defence; it is fictitious if the capture loses to a pin, discovered line or recapture.
A fictitious threat still ties the opponent and becomes real the moment it is forgotten.
A move that removes the opponent's counterplay first pays only when his threat is genuine and he can execute it.
contrasts: A piece left en prise is safe for a few moves; later the same capture works because the position changed.
Spending a tempo to disarm a threat that did not exist (prophylaxis as passivity).
A position with nothing attacked; the correct answer is that there is no threat.

soft_prereq_notes.SAF.LOOSE.D2: whether a piece is loose changes which threats are real
